title: The Shallow Immutability Trap: Why Your Java Records Aren't Safe in Production
description: Java records promise immutability, but shallow copy mechanics can expose your production systems to silent data corruption. Learn how to master JEP 395 validation patterns.
content:
## Introduction

Imagine you are running an e-commerce platform during a flash sale. Your system processes hundreds of orders per second. To prevent race conditions and ensure data integrity, you refactored your core domain models from mutable POJOs to modern Java records. You felt secure knowing that records are immutable. Suddenly, the monitoring dashboard lights up with alerts. Customers are checking out with negative order totals, bypassing payment validation. 

How did this happen? A downstream inventory thread modified a shared list of items inside an order after the order passed through your validation checks. Even though you used a record, your application state mutated silently. 

We can trace the roots of this behavior to Java Platform JEP 395, which formally introduced records to the language as transparent carriers for immutable data. While JEP 395 simplifies our codebases by eliminating boilerplate, it also introduces subtle design limitations that trip up even experienced engineers. After reading this article, you will understand how records manage state under the hood, how to implement validation patterns that actually protect your application, and how to handle mutable references without degrading system performance.

> Most engineers assume that declaring a Java record automatically makes all of its nested data structures immutable, but the real issue is that records only guarantee shallow immutability of their direct fields.

## The Core Idea

To understand why our flash-sale bug occurred, we must examine what a record actually is. JEP 395 defines records as "nominal tuples." They are not just a convenient replacement for Lombok's `@Value` annotation or boilerplate getters. Instead, they represent a mathematical commitment: the API of a record is its state, and its state is its API.

Have you ever wondered why Java records do not allow you to extend other classes, or why all of their fields are implicitly final? This design choice guarantees that a record is nothing more than the sum of its parts. However, the final modifier on a Java field only restricts the reassignment of the reference itself. It does nothing to protect the internal state of the object that the reference points to.

To visualize this, imagine a laminated index card. Once you write an address on this card and laminate it, you cannot change the text written on the card. The reference is fixed. But what if the text you wrote is a URL pointing to a public Google Doc? Anyone with the link can still open the document and edit the text inside it. The laminated card itself remains unchanged, but the data it points to has mutated. 

This is shallow immutability. If your record contains a standard `java.util.List`, `java.util.Map`, or a custom mutable class, any code with a reference to those objects can mutate them at any time. The record's final field still points to the same list instance, but the list's contents have changed.

### The Compact Constructor Mechanics

To defend against this vulnerability, we must use the compact constructor. In a traditional Java class, you write a constructor that accepts arguments and manually assigns them to fields using `this.x = x`. Records introduce a shorthand called the compact constructor, which omits the parameter list entirely.

Under the hood, the compiler does something unique here. It does not immediately assign the values to the record's final fields when the compact constructor block begins. Instead, it allows you to validate and transform the incoming parameters *before* any assignment happens. At the end of the compact constructor block, the compiler automatically generates the field assignments using the final state of those parameters. This distinction is critical for implementing defensive copying safely.

## Code Walkthrough

### Securing a Record Against Shared Mutability

Let us look at how to correctly implement validation and defensive copying inside a compact constructor. We want to ensure that once we construct our `Order` record, no external thread can mutate its list of items, and no one can initialize it with invalid data.

```java
package com.example.sales;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Objects;

public record Order(String orderId, List<OrderItem> items) {
    
    public Order {
        Objects.requireNonNull(orderId, "Order ID must not be null");
        if (items == null || items.isEmpty()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Order must contain at least one item");
        }
        
        // We reassign the incoming parameter, not the final field.
        // List.copyOf creates an unmodifiable copy and rejects null elements.
        items = List.copyOf(items);
    }
}
```

Let us trace what happens when a client calls `new Order("123", mutableList)`. 

First, the runtime executes our validation checks. If the order ID is null or the list of items is empty, we immediately throw an exception, preventing the creation of an invalid object. 

Second, we reassign the local parameter `items` using `List.copyOf(items)`. This method creates a new, unmodifiable list containing the same elements. If someone subsequently modifies the original `mutableList` passed into the constructor, our record remains completely unaffected because it points to the new, isolated copy. 

Third, notice that we did not write `this.items = List.copyOf(items)`. If you attempt to write that inside a compact constructor, the compiler will flag it as an error because you cannot assign values to final instance fields here. The compiler handle those assignments automatically at the very end of the block, using whatever value our local `items` parameter holds at that moment.

## Where This Goes Wrong in Production

### The Jackson Deserialization Trap

When we integrate records with JSON libraries like Jackson, we often run into issues with default configuration settings. By default, Jackson deserializes JSON arrays into mutable `ArrayList` instances. If your API accepts a record containing a list, and you do not implement defensive copying in your compact constructor, Jackson will inject a mutable list into your record. If downstream services modify this list during request processing, you will pollute your application state. To fix this, you must enforce defensive copying in the compact constructor or register custom deserializers that map JSON arrays directly to immutable collection types.

### Performance Degradation in High-Throughput Pipelines

While defensive copying preserves data integrity, it introduces a performance tax. If you process millions of messages per second from a Kafka topic and defensively copy nested collections inside every record constructor, you will flood the JVM heap with short-lived objects. This triggers frequent garbage collection pauses, which degrades your system's throughput. To mitigate this, you should avoid defensive copying when you can guarantee that the producer of the collection is trusted and will not mutate it. Alternatively, you can define a package-private constructor that skips the copy step for internal, performance-sensitive pipelines while keeping the public constructor safe.

### The Hibernate Identity Crisis

Engineers often try to use records directly as JPA/Hibernate entities because they want to eliminate boilerplate. However, Hibernate relies on subclassing and proxying to implement dirty checking and lazy loading. Because records are implicitly `final`, Hibernate cannot create proxies for them. Furthermore, Hibernate expects entities to have mutable identifiers and lifecycle states that the persistence context can manage. Trying to force records into this model leads to detached entity state bugs and unexpected database roundtrips. The proper fix is to keep your JPA entities as traditional classes and map them to records only at your service boundary as read-only Data Transfer Objects (DTOs).

If you discuss records in a technical interview, you can stand out by moving beyond the typical "boilerplate reduction" explanation. Explain how records compile to nominal tuples and discuss the shallow immutability of nested collections. Describe how the compact constructor compiles down to parameter reassignment rather than direct field assignment, showing that you understand the JVM specification rather than just the syntax.

## Key Takeaways

* Reassign parameters directly within the compact constructor to safely transform or copy data before the compiler binds those values to the record's final fields.
* Prevent shared-state mutation by replacing legacy mutable types like `java.util.Date` with modern immutable alternatives like `java.time.Instant` in your record components.
* Use `List.copyOf` or `Map.copyOf` to create true unmodifiable copies of collections, rather than wrappers like `Collections.unmodifiableList` which still reflect changes made to the underlying source list.
* Avoid using records as JPA/Hibernate entities; instead, use them as read-only DTOs at your service boundaries to keep your database entities separate from your data transmission contracts.
* Profile your application's garbage collection behavior before implementing deep defensive copies in high-throughput loops to ensure you are not creating excessive memory pressure.
* Remember that records do not support inheritance because their state header must remain the complete, unalterable definition of the type.
